Replay

Using the new Replay bridge in Scrapyard

4 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Data and lifetime boundaryImprovements driven by actual useMeasured tradeoffsVerification and remaining scope

This record covers Scrapyard's initial authoring-bridge integration for enemies, loot and gameplay audio, including its lifetime changes, measured presentation costs and focused checks. For the current scene composition, follow the editor-first guide. The original sibling game remains separate; the measurements below do not cover every adapter.

Data and lifetime boundary#

shared/presentation/mobs.odin projects the selected observed World into detached mob display values: appearance, health, telegraph, status tint and nearby-prey information. No World or mutable catalog pointer enters a Godot rig. Existing observed interpolation remains the sampling policy for enemies and loot; local players and projectiles retain their current prediction policy.

scripts/mob_bridge.odin binds those values through View_Pool2. A PackedScene supplies Body and Telegraph children; attach caches them once. Paint handles data changes; frame handles animation. Generation, epoch, floor/run, observation reset and backward-time boundaries retire stale rigs. Initial/late observations seed health silently rather than inventing damage feedback. Loot uses the same typed lifetime owner with its existing authored scrap scene.

Before, the game precreated 64 enemy sprites plus 64 telegraph rings and 128 scrap scenes (three nodes each), then manually hid unused slots and reset their state. The bridge removes those 512 eagerly reserved nodes. Live entities instantiate views on demand, and recycled simulation slots get new scene lifetimes. Existing actor tests now check retirement and absence of stale state on the replacement, rather than requiring the same engine object to survive unrelated entities.

This changes the pooling tradeoff: lifecycle safety and lower idle node count come with scene creation/free on membership churn. The timing below measures steady presentation, not that creation cost. High-churn projectiles should be evaluated separately before migration.

Improvements driven by actual use#

Two missing shared primitives became apparent:

  1. Animation separate from changed-data painting. A stationary enemy still animates. View_Binding.frame and view_pool_frame advance presentation time without putting a render delta/frame counter in the display payload or forcing every binding to repaint. It visits only live entries and animates children.
  2. Audio projection with occurrence context. Scrapyard derives pitch from a stable event ID and reconstructs hurt positions at the event tick. The new audio_route_init_change callback receives the complete Change, removing the need for an implicit current-event side channel. It uses the existing route's policy, one-shot ledger, cancellation and epoch handling.

scripts/audio.odin now routes gameplay changes through Audio_Route. Music fades and sounds inferred from state remain game-specific, sharing the route's voice pool where appropriate. No audio or view state is added to World/checkpoints.

Measured tradeoffs#

An isolated headless benchmark compares the frozen previous game adapter with the new adapter. Both paint the same detached frames through the real game paint function, with identical catalogs, mixed enemy kinds and one drop per enemy. Three alternating process pairs per size use warmup plus five 120-call batches. Simulation state is checked unchanged after every benchmark. Builds do not overlap measurement. These are native CPU presentation timings, not rendered FPS or GPU measurements. Both builds use the same framework version and the build helper's default -debug flags, with no SCRIPT_BUILD_FLAGS optimization override. Release-build timings can differ.

Enemies and drops, each Previous paint New paint
0 76.05 µs 75.71 µs
8 81.05 µs 84.32 µs
32 85.04 µs 96.84 µs

The 32-entity case adds about 11.8 µs, or 14% of this isolated paint call. Typed projection, comparison and ownership work is measurable. This integration is not a general performance win. Its value here is explicit lifetimes and a smaller, testable Godot boundary, plus fewer unused nodes. It also adds setup and projection code; animation rules remain game code. There is no line-count or human productivity superiority claim.

The complete observed World is still used elsewhere in Scrapyard's paint function. Detached mob values reduce what rigs receive; they do not remove all World copies from the game or change history memory. The callbacks receive copied display data and the bridge manages scene lifetimes. Future conversions should measure their own costs.

Verification and remaining scope#

Focused checks pass for enemy attack/hit/death, fresh lifetime replacement, player animation compatibility, damage/pickup effects and floor cleanup; contextual wound audio position/pitch/once-only behavior; and host/client/observer combat with 120 ms latency and equal whole-world hashes. The game scripts compile for WASM. Shared Godot tests verify unchanged-value animation and contextual route cancellation. The projection test verifies detached values and generation handles.

No existing gameplay/shared-model or Kit source changed. Native/WASM compilation is not a new browser execution or hardware-audio listening claim. This increment does not repeat the full migration/parity matrix.

Player rigs, predicted projectile selection, bespoke particles, input/UI bindings and Resource catalog loading remain on their current adapters. Convert these only where another concrete integration yields a useful simplification. In particular, projectile selection may need multiple identity domains when predicted and observed pools diverge; do not force that into one ambiguous view pool.

Shell
REPLAY_SCRAP_BRIDGE_OUT=/absolute/fresh/output \
  nix develop --command bash tests/replay_scrapyard_bridge/run.sh

Source and test receipts record the exact workload, initial fixture failures and preserved original sources.
